[Button: i] Ilustrace: radyz.cz, AI vizualizace Projekt HISTOR zpřístupnil dataset definic nástrojů MCP a jejich změn. Snapshot z 20. října obsahuje přes 81 tisíc evidovaných serverů a balíčků a téměř 24 tisíc zaznamenaných změn. U vzdálených serverů sleduje deklarované nástroje, u balíčků npm a PyPI je získává spuštěním v sandboxu. Data lze použít ke studiu toho, jak se rozhraní nástrojů pro AI agenty vyvíjejí. Soubory obsahují definice, historii změn i výsledky pomocných kontrol a mají zveřejněné kontrolní součty a podepsaný manifest. Dataset je dostupný pod CC BY 4.0. Autoři výslovně varují, že změna definice ani shoda s podezřelým vzorem nedokazuje škodlivost serveru. This indicates that the Engine ECM is not responding to command. Port Engine Commands 12917 7 The MCP is not receiving Engine Speed or Desired Engine Speed from the PORT -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- HISTOR — transparency log for MCP tool definitions (https://alexar76.github.io/histor/) citeturn81search1 [wordlim: 200] Crawled: yesterday; Read → digest → label → append → sign → compare ## How the log works Six steps, every one of them checkable by someone who does not trust HISTOR. The only thing you have to take on faith is that the observation happened when the label says it did — and the log makes it impossible to change that story afterwards. 01 ### Read Remote endpoints in the official MCP registry: initialize, then tools/list, drained across every page; no tool is called, and private addresses are refused before the connection opens. npm and PyPI packages: installed and started in the sandbox described below, with no route out. 02 ### Digest The tool set is reduced to name, description, input and output schema, sorted by UTF-16 code units and hashed over its RFC 8785 canonical form. Anyone holding the same tools gets the same digest — which is what makes a comparison possible. 03 ### Label Four MTL/1 methods, one signed AWR/2 document each: what was observed, what the WARDEN pattern set matched, whether the definitions changed since the last label, and whether the name is on a threat list. No score, ever. 04 ### Append Every label becomes a leaf of an RFC 9162 Merkle tree: leaf hash = SHA-256(0x00 ‖ JCS(label)). The label you download is the leaf input, so you can recompute its hash yourself. 05 ### Sign After each crawl HISTOR signs a tree head: the size and the root. Keep yesterday's head; ask for a consistency proof to today's; if anything was removed or rewritten, the proof fails. 06 ### Compare Each day a continuity label compares the new digest with the last one. Equal: "unchanged since". Different: a change, with the date and a per-tool diff. A client that checks what it received adds the view no crawler has. Where an npm or PyPI package is run ## Test conditions A package observation is true for these conditions, and no others. Every package page names the exact image it ran in and any configuration it was given. ### System Linux x86_64, inside gVisor (runsc): the package talks to a kernel written for sandboxing, not to the host's. An unprivileged user, no capabilities, a read-only root. ### Runtimes npm packages in histor-node:22, PyPI packages in histor-python:3.12: the official node:22-bookworm-slim and python:3.12-slim images plus bash, git, Python 3 or Node 22 and a Java 21 runtime — never Docker — built when a sandbox host is installed. A package whose Requires-Python excludes 3.12 runs on histor-python:3.13 or 3.14; one that requires a newer Node runs again on histor-node:24. The exact image a package ran in is on its page. ### Install npm with --ignore-scripts, then the install scripts in a traced stage of their own. PyPI: wheels only — a package that ships only source is reported, never built. ### Network No route out. Every name the package looks up resolves to HISTOR's own traps, which record what was sent and forward nothing. A server that needs the internet to start shows that here. ### Secrets None are real. Decoy credentials sit in HOME and a decoy .env in the working directory. A variable the package says it needs gets a placeholder; where the placeholder was sent is recorded. ### Limits 512 MB of memory, one CPU, 64 MB of /tmp. 360 s to install, 150 s to start and answer; up to 15 tools called once each with canary arguments, 8 s per call. ### Configuration Only names: required variables its registry entry declares or that it printed when it exited, and a start argument such as serve when its usage text offers one. Never a value from anyone else. ## What a label does not say The profile HISTOR implements forbids the words safe, secure, audited, certified, approved and trusted. Here is why, in the terms of what the log can and cannot show. ### Not a safety rating A pattern match is a reason to read a definition, not a finding. Three of the four methods can never return fail. There is no score to rank by, because no score HISTOR could compute would mean what a reader takes it to mean. ### Not the code Labels are about advertised text. A remote endpoint's source is never read and its tools are never invoked; a package runs only in the sandbox, against nothing real. A server can keep identical definitions and behave differently for real users; the log cannot see that, and says so inside every label. ### A change is not an accusation A version bump changes definitions too. A change is shown as a date and a diff, in amber, never red. What you do with it is yours: re-read, re-approve, or pin the old digest. ### A package as run here, not on your machine An npm or PyPI server is observed under the test conditions above: Linux, no internet, placeholder keys. One that needs Windows, a real account or the network may show fewer tools or none; its page says why it exited. ### One operator, one key Today one party runs the log. A second observer on another network is the next step, and any AIMarket hub can run one. Until then, what the key proves is who said it — not that it is true. ### Behind a login, unseen Endpoints that require authentication answer 401 to everyone without a key, including HISTOR. They are counted and listed as not observed, never dropped from the numbers. For clients, registries and server authors ## Use it Before your agent trusts a server, send the tools it received. The answer is signed by the log's did:key and names the tree head it was given under. curl -sS https://histor.modelmarket.dev/api/v1/check \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"endpoint":"https://example.com/mcp","tools":[ …tools/list result… ],"contribute":true}' # -> {"type":"histor.check/v1","match":"same"|"different"|"previously-observed"|…, # "observed":{"unchangedSince":"…","changes":0}, "patternScan":{…}, "signature":{…}} # README badge for your server [![MCP tool defs](https://histor.modelmarket.dev/badge/.svg)](https://histor.modelmarket.dev/s/) # Atom feed of every observed change https://histor.modelmarket.dev/feed.xml WARDEN checks definitions at connect HISTOR remembers what was advertised THEMIS admits at publish Hub lists histor.check@v1 AWR the signed format ## Questions Is this a marketplace listing? No. The server list is the log's index: every remote endpoint in the official MCP registry, with what HISTOR could observe about it. Nothing here is for sale and nothing is ranked by quality. Does HISTOR tell me a server is safe? No, and it never will. It tells you what a server advertised, whether that changed, and which published patterns matched the text. Whether to trust the server is your decision — HISTOR makes sure you decide on the same facts as everyone else. Why are so many servers "not observed"? Most remote MCP endpoints require a login (they answer 401 to anyone without a key), some use the legacy SSE transport or need per-user values in the URL, and some are simply down. They stay on the list with the reason, so the numbers never hide them. How do I check a server I already use? Open the Check tab, paste the server's endpoint and the tools/list result your client received, and press Check. You get back, signed, whether HISTOR observed the same definitions — or different ones, or an older set. How do I get a badge for my server? Find your endpoint on the Servers tab, open it, and copy the Markdown snippet under the facts. The badge shows the date your definitions were pinned or last changed, and links to the full history. Why should I trust HISTOR itself? You do not have to. Every label and every tree head is signed with one published key; the Log tab proves in your browser that the log only grew; and the command-line auditor does the same from any machine. What remains is that one operator runs it today — a second, independent observer is the next step. What does it cost? Looking things up, the badges, the feed and /check are free. HISTOR also offers histor.check@v1 to the AIMarket Hub, so agents can reach it through the market. I run an MCP server. What does HISTOR send it, and how do I opt out? Once a day: initialize, notifications/initialized and tools/list — never a tool call, never a redirect followed, at most two connections per host, from a User-Agent that starts with histor/. To be left out, open an issue on the histor repository with your endpoint or host; it is then listed as not observed (operator-opt-out), with the reason, rather than silently dropped.
